title: Castle Pines Village Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Castle Pines Village wells have a 474-foot median depth, with finished costs modeled at $29,700-$45,100.
h1: Wells in Castle Pines Village, Colorado
intro_html:
Well records within 5 miles of Castle Pines Village show a wide range of drilling conditions. The median reported depth is 474 feet, and the middle half runs from 255 to 650 feet. Most reported yields are usable for household wells, with a median of 12.0 gallons per minute.

This area includes Castle Pines, Sedalia, Castle Rock, Louviers, Lone Tree and Stepping Stone. The records point to Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock as the main drilling setting, with fractured-bedrock and Denver Basin aquifers named on permits. Use these figures to screen a property, then have a driller evaluate the specific lot.

sections.heading: Castle Pines Village well depth is often substantial
sections.html:
Among wells with a reported total depth, the median is 474 feet. The middle half extends from 255 to 650 feet, so a drilling bid based only on the median can miss the conditions at a particular lot. The 90th percentile is 1,014 feet, and the deepest record reaches 3,220 feet.

Depths are spread across the area: 37% are between 300 and 600 feet, while 33% are 600 feet or deeper. Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock, changing formations and the target aquifer all affect the final depth. Neighboring permits are useful for planning, but they do not guarantee the same result on your parcel.

sections.heading: Most Castle Pines Village wells make useful water
sections.html:
Reported pump yields have a median of 12.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 10.0 and 15.0 gallons per minute. The records show 67% producing between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, and 32% producing more than 15 gallons per minute.

Only 1% report yields between 1 and 5 gallons per minute, and 0% are under 1 gallon per minute. That is encouraging for typical household planning, but a yield test is still important. Pump size, storage, irrigation demand and the well permit determine how much water can actually be used. An exempt household-use well is subject to Colorado’s 35 gallons-per-minute pumping limit.

sections.heading: Water levels show a deeper recent measurement pattern
sections.html:
The median static water level is 360 feet below the surface, with the middle half from 195 to 546 feet. This is the depth to water when the well is not being pumped, not the total well depth. It matters for pump setting, electrical planning and the cost of servicing the well.

Measurements by decade were 222 feet in the 1970s, 298 feet in the 1980s, 432 feet in the 2010s and 360 feet in the 2020s. That series shows deeper reported water levels in the later period than in the earlier records, but the measurements are limited to 132 wells and do not by themselves prove a uniform, continuing decline across Castle Pines Village.

sections.heading: Permit history points to a long-established drilling area
sections.html:
Colorado DWR records contain 2,714 permitted wells within the local study area. Of those, 1,416 are recorded as constructed, 1,556 report a total depth and 875 report a pump yield. The newest permit year is 2025, with 13 permits issued in the 2020s.

Hier Drilling Co Inc, listed with Bruce A. Hier, appears most often with 725 records. Hier Drilling Co., listed with Peter J. Hier, appears on 285, and records marked Authorized appear on 161. These names describe permit history, not a recommendation. Confirm current licensing, insurance, scope and references before hiring a driller.

sections.heading: A median-depth Castle Pines Village well costs real money
sections.html:
The local cost model uses a drilling rate of $50-$70 per foot in Denver Basin sedimentary bedrock. At the 474-foot median depth, the drilled hole is modeled at about $23,700-$33,100. A finished system with pump, pressure tank, trenching and electrical is modeled at about $29,700-$45,100.

Those figures are planning ranges, not a guaranteed bid. A deeper-than-typical hole, difficult access, casing and grout requirements, water-level conditions or extra trenching can change the total. Ask each contractor to separate drilling, casing, grout, development, pump equipment, electrical work and connection to the house so competing bids can be compared accurately.

sections.heading: Check water quality, yield and site constraints before closing
sections.html:
Mapped environmental records within about 10 miles include 71 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 28 historic mine features and 16 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. These mapped sites do not establish contamination on a specific parcel, but they are a reason to review the location and test the well water. A licensed laboratory should test for the contaminants relevant to the property and its surroundings.

Also investigate low-yield risk, dry-hole risk and the location of septic and replacement areas. Septic setbacks, driveway access, building placement and the well’s permitted use need to work together. In an over-appropriated basin, a new well may require an augmentation plan or other water-right review. Read the permit conditions before assuming a well can serve a new home, livestock or irrigation.

sections.heading: Use nearby permits to screen a lot before you build
sections.html:
Start with the well permits closest to the parcel, then compare depth, reported yield, static water level, aquifer name and drilling date. Castle Pines is about 2 miles away, Sedalia about 4 miles, and Castle Rock about 5 miles; Louviers, Lone Tree and Stepping Stone are each about 6 miles. These areas provide context, but the nearest well is usually more useful than a broad regional average.

For a purchase, make the contract and due-diligence period long enough to inspect the well, collect a water sample and verify the permit. For a build, obtain a site-specific drilling and access estimate before finalizing the house location. Plan the well, septic field, driveway, electrical route and backup access as one site layout, not as separate afterthoughts.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Castle Pines Village?
faq.a: The median reported well depth within 5 miles of Castle Pines Village is 474 feet. The middle half ranges from 255 to 650 feet. About 33% of wells are 600 feet or deeper, and the deepest record is 3,220 feet. A nearby well can help with planning, but local geology can produce a different depth on your lot.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a well in Castle Pines Village?
faq.a: The local model uses $50-$70 per foot. At the 474-foot median depth, drilling the hole is estimated at $23,700-$33,100. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is estimated at $29,700-$45,100. Access, depth, casing, grout and site-specific electrical or trenching needs can move the final bid.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Castle Pines Village?
faq.a: Reported pump yields have a median of 12.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 10.0 and 15.0 gallons per minute. About 67% produce between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, while 32% produce more than 15 gallons per minute. A yield test and the well permit are still needed for a specific property.

faq.q: Is well water safe in Castle Pines Village?
faq.a: The well records do not establish whether a particular home’s water is safe. Within about 10 miles, mapped records include 71 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 28 historic mine features and 16 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test the well through a licensed laboratory and review nearby environmental records before relying on the water.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping in Castle Pines Village?
faq.a: Reported median static water levels were 222 feet in the 1970s, 298 feet in the 1980s, 432 feet in the 2010s and 360 feet in the 2020s. The later measurements are deeper than the earliest period, but only 132 wells report static water levels. That pattern does not prove a uniform continuing decline across the area.
